heading: How Florida defines air-conditioning contractors

items.label: Class A
items.text: The statute defines a Class A air-conditioning contractor as
items.quote: a contractor whose services are unlimited in the execution of contracts requiring the experience, knowledge, and skill to install, maintain, repair, fabricate, alter, extend, or design, if not prohibited by law, central air-conditioning, refrigeration, heating, and ventilating systems

items.label: Class B
items.text: A Class B air-conditioning contractor is
items.quote: a contractor whose services are limited to 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 Btu of heating in any one system

items.label: Wiring
items.quote: repair or replace power wiring, disconnects, breakers, or fuses for dedicated HVAC circuits with proper use of a circuit breaker lock

items.label: Excluded work
items.text: For both classes, the scope of work
items.quote: does not include any work such as liquefied petroleum or natural gas fuel lines within buildings, except for disconnecting or reconnecting changeouts of liquefied petroleum or natural gas appliances within buildings; potable water lines or connections thereto; sanitary sewer lines; swimming pool piping and filters; or electrical power wiring

items.label: Class C
items.text: Class C is closed to new applicants:
items.quote: Only a person who was registered or certified as a Class C air-conditioning contractor as of October 1, 1988, shall be so registered or certified after October 1, 1988.

originShared.text: Florida's Reciprocity form (DBPR CILB 32) covers applicants from Louisiana, Mississippi, and North Carolina in General, Building, and Residential categories; it has no Air-Conditioning category, so reciprocity is not available to HVAC contractors in Florida.
The route is DBPR CILB 10, Certification by Endorsement (Section 489.115(3), Florida Statutes), which lists Class A and Class B Air-Conditioning among its license categories.

Within CILB 10, the NASCLA-based Option A does not apply to this classification: the form restricts it to "General, Building, and Residential license" only. The route is Option C: hold a valid, current out-of-state license for at least 10 years, active now or within the last 2 years, of a license type "the same or similar as the license type being applied for".

Options A (substantially equivalent exam) and B (substantially equivalent licensing criteria) also exist, but CILB 10 warns that comparisons of state-specific tests are "very stringent and rarely approved".
For Option C, submit verification of licensure from your state showing at least 10 years and any disciplinary action, and a copy of your state's statutes or rules defining your license type.

Open question: CILB 10's 2-hour Florida Building Code course is required of General, Building, Residential, and Roofing Contractor applicants; Air-Conditioning is not listed, and the document does not say whether Air-Conditioning applicants face it.
